panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: Dorsal view of both hands of the reported patient with Jacobsen syndrome, showing the short, tapered fingers described in the caption as a dysmorphic limb feature of the disease. Article title and in-text mentions tie these hand changes directly to Jacobsen syndrome. B: Palmar view of the same patient's hands demonstrating the short, tapered fingers reported as part of the Jacobsen syndrome phenotype in the caption and in-text description. C: Full-body clinical photograph of the reported Jacobsen syndrome patient showing a short neck and the characteristic backward head-reclined posture attributed to palpebral ptosis, both explicitly linked to the disease in the caption and in-text.
panels.attribution_text: Brum et al. Jacobsen syndrome associated with Shone's complex: a case report.. Revista paulista de pediatria : orgao oficial da Sociedade de Pediatria de Sao Paulo 2025. doi:10.1590/1984-0462/2025/43/2024136. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 2.
panels.figure_caption: View of the hands and whole body, showing alterations in other regions of the body. Back of hands (A) and palm of hands (B): hands with short, tapered fingers; full body view (C): short neck and often adopts a posture with the head slightly reclined backward, possibly attributable to eyelid ptosis.
in_text_mentions: us, ptosis, downward-sloping palpebral fissure, long philtrum, wide nasal bridge, anteverted nostril, thin lips, low-set and downward-sloping eyebrows, low-set and posteriorly rotated ears, trigonocephaly, as well as alterations in other parts of the body such as a short neck, and short and tapered hands and fingers, and often adopts a posture with the head slightly reclined backward, possibly due to palpebral ptosis. Some of these features can be seen in Figures 1 and 2. In addition, she has a speech delay, being able to pronounce a few words, even with her mother, of the same foreign origin.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: Fetal ultrasound shows an interventricular septal defect, a congenital cardiac defect reported in Jacobsen syndrome; the article title and panel-specific caption support disease attribution. B: Color Doppler fetal ultrasound demonstrates septal blood flow across the ventricular septal defect, supporting a congenital cardiac defect in this Jacobsen syndrome case. C: Fetal ultrasound shows left renal pelvis widening, a renal anomaly described in Jacobsen syndrome; article title and specific caption support attribution. D: Fetal color Doppler ultrasound shows a single umbilical artery, a nonspecific prenatal finding in this Jacobsen syndrome case; it is not represented in the allowed vocabulary, so it is proposed as a finding.

panels.figure_caption: Prenatal ultrasound at 22 weeks of gestation showing: A: Interventricular septal defect; B: Presence of septal blood flow; C: Left renal pelvis widening; D: Single umbilical artery.
in_text_mentions: the head circumference was 19.8 cm, the abdominal circumference was 16.6 cm, the femur length was 3.8 cm, and the amniotic fluid index was 13.3 cm. The main abnormal manifestations on the ultrasound images included an interventricular septal defect, the presence of septal blood flow, dilation of the left renal pelvis, and a single umbilical artery (Fig. 1). After genetic counseling, the woman was offered amniocentesis for cytogenetic and single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) array analysis at 23 weeks of gestation because of advanced age in combination with these abnormal ultrasound indicators.

A: Axial T1 MRI of the brain in a patient with Jacobsen syndrome, showing hypomyelination in parieto-occipital white matter and genu of corpus callosum, with reduced basal ganglia conspicuity. The finding is not covered by the provided finding vocabulary, so it is recorded as proposed findings. B: Axial T2 MRI of the brain in the same patient with Jacobsen syndrome, showing white matter hypomyelination in parieto-occipital regions and the genu of the corpus callosum. The finding is not represented in the supplied vocabulary, so it is recorded as proposed findings.

panels.figure_caption: MRI findings of white matter hypomyelination Axial T1 (A) and T2 (B) images at six months demonstrating hypomyelination in parieto-occipital white matter (yellow arrows) and genu of corpus callosum (red arrows), as well as reduced conspicuity of basal ganglia (blue arrows).
in_text_mentions: As part of the investigations into hypotonia and developmental delay, a magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan was performed a few days after the chromosomal microarray analysis. MRI brain was performed on a 1.5T scanner using axial T1-weighted, T2-weighted, FLAIR, and DWI/ADC sequences. Axial T2, as well as axial T1, shows diffuse delayed myelination predominantly in the parieto-occipital white matter and genu of corpus callosum; there was no structural malformation (Figure 2).

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: Chest radiograph from a neonate with Jacobsen syndrome showing captioned pulmonary abnormalities (atelectasis and diffuse opacifications); the disease link is supported by the disease-focused case report title and panel-specific caption, though the findings are not in the provided vocabulary. B: Second chest radiograph from the same neonate with Jacobsen syndrome, showing captioned pulmonary abnormalities; disease attribution is supported by the case report title and caption, with findings outside the provided vocabulary. C: Chest CT from a neonate with Jacobsen syndrome showing captioned atelectasis, septal thickening, and ground-glass opacities; attribution is supported by the disease-focused case report title and panel-specific caption, but these pulmonary findings are not in the provided vocabulary.
panels.attribution_text: Dalen et al. Neonatal interstitial lung disease in a girl with Jacobsen syndrome: a case report.. Journal of medical case reports 2022. doi:10.1186/s13256-022-03351-5. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: A–C Radiographs of the lungs acquired with a few hours interval on DOL 9 show: A, B intermittent atelectasis (black arrowhead) of the right upper lobe and central diffuse opacifications bilaterally (white arrows). A chest computed tomography (CT) at DOL 10 revealed: C Substantial atelectasis in the dorsal segments of the lungs (black arrowheads) and signs of thickened interlobular septae (black arrows) and scattered ground-glass opacifications (white arrows)
in_text_mentions: XF1). Radiologic investigations, including a chest computed tomography (CT) at DOL 10, revealed intermittent atelectasis, ground-glass opacifications, and signs of thickened interlobular septae (Fig. 1). A lung wedge biopsy at DOL 22 showed delayed maturation and relatively pronounced interstitial glycogenosis, consistent with PIG (Fig. 2). Four days prior to the biopsy she had suffered severe clinical deterioration and was given a single high dose of dexamethasone (750 µg), which had a striking clinical effect.
